strengths: Addresses important gap in benchmarking: focuses on end-to-end data science pipeline generation over realistic data lakes, unlike prior benchmarks focused on individual components
Well-designed benchmark with thoughtful curation: 104 manually-validated tasks grounded in published domain analyses, spanning 6 diverse domains with 1700 real data files from 24 sources

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: three different automation settings (end-to-end, design, implementation) provide nuanced assessment of system capabilities; 633 subtasks enable granular analysis

Useful multi-perspective evaluation design: reveals interesting insights like models performing better on pipeline design than implementation (Table 6), suggesting reasoning limitations vs. execution capability
Reproducibility: reference solutions provided and commitment to release code and benchmark; detailed methodology description
Rigorous task validation: independent annotators reconstruct pipelines to identify ambiguities; clear differentiation from prior work shown in Table 1
weaknesses: Unfair evaluation of proprietary systems: OpenAI Deep Research given internet access and restricted file constraints while DS-GURU processes full data lakes; acknowledged but still presented as comparable, raising concerns about data leakage from published papers (Table 5)

Limited methodological novelty: DS-GURU is straightforward application of existing techniques (chain-of-thought, iterative error correction); no novel methods for data discovery or schema understanding

Shallow error analysis: limited investigation of failure modes beyond noting astronomy tasks are harder; no systematic categorization of error types or analysis of task characteristics predicting failure

Incomplete implementation details: data sampling strategy described as 'heuristically chosen' without specific thresholds; no ablation studies on prompt engineering variations beyond three DS-GURU variants

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-based code evaluation for pipeline design (Section 3.2) susceptible to hallucination with no reported reliability validation; multiple heterogeneous scoring metrics (exact match, F1, RAE, ParaPluie) complicate aggregation; no statistical significance testing

Potential data leakage issues: acknowledged problem with wildfire domain showing inflated performance due to pre-training exposure; no comprehensive analysis of training data overlap with published source materials
Dataset scale limitations: 104 end-to-end tasks is relatively small for modern standards, potentially limiting fine-tuning approaches; marked heterogeneity in task difficulty not fully characterized

Incomplete presentation: repository URLs missing in multiple places; model naming inconsistencies (GPT-o3); Table 8 appears incomplete with minimal discussion; key details relegated to supplementary material

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Comprehensively evaluates end-to-end data-to-insight pipelines, whereas prior work focuses on isolated steps
Rigorous benchmark construction: 104 carefully curated tasks with double-annotation validation and reference implementations; real-world grounding in published studies
Appropriate scale and scope: 1700 data files from 24 sources across 6 domains, with clear documentation and mix of difficulty levels
Multi-level evaluation framework: Three automation settings (end-to-end, design, implementation) provide nuanced capability assessment
Broad empirical evaluation: Tests 8 different systems with meaningful comparisons across variants and models
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DS-GURU applies only standard techniques (chain-of-thought prompting, data sampling, iterative error correction) without methodological innovation; framework contribution is minimal
Questionable data sampling strategy: 'First N rows' approach lacks justification and is problematic for real data science where temporal/hierarchical ordering matters; no sensitivity analysis

Unfair baseline comparisons: OpenAI Deep Research restricted to 10 files but permitted web search (authors note possible bias from fetching published papers, Table 5); DS-GURU processes full data lakes—comparisons not directly comparable

Shallow analysis and missing investigations: (1) No detailed error categorization or failure mode analysis; (2) Unexplained gaps between pipeline design (41.6%) and implementation (19.75%) performance suggest design isn't bottleneck; (3) Large domain variance (wildfire 50.7% vs astronomy 3.5%) discussed but not investigated
Absent human baseline: No evaluation of domain expert performance or task solvability ceiling; critical for assessing task ambiguity and benchmark validity

Evaluation methodology concerns: Multiple fine-grained metrics in Table 8 (bleu, code(L2), f1, mean_abs, etc.) reported without clear definitions, suggesting metric fishing; Relative Absolute Error undefined at y=0; choice of metrics not justified

Incomplete experimental rigor: No ablation studies on design choices (sampling strategy, iteration count, decomposition approach); token budgets 'heuristically chosen' without details; reproducibility concerns despite promised code release
Limited baseline sophistication: No comparison to modern agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGen) or retrieval-augmented generation; only 2 proprietary systems tested with fairness issues
Artificial data discovery task: Real data scientists have domain knowledge and metadata access; forcing discovery from 1764 raw files may overweight an artificial capability

Task ambiguity not fully addressed: Example tasks reference implicit domain knowledge ('linearly interpolate'); double-annotation mitigates but doesn't eliminate inherent ambiguity; no inter-annotator agreement reported
Superficial insights: Main findings ('LLMs struggle with complex multi-step tasks requiring data discovery') are intuitive; paper reports numbers without explaining why or proposing solutions
Presentation issues: Incomplete sentence on page 3 ('available a'); Figure 1 duplicated; Table 8 difficult to parse with missing entries; code/data availability promised but not confirmed

strengths: Addresses clear gap in literature by focusing on end-to-end data science pipelines rather than individual pipeline steps; existing benchmarks evaluate components in isolation
High-quality benchmark construction with manual curation, independent annotator validation, real scientific studies as grounding, and reference implementations for all 104 tasks
Realistic, challenging datasets with 1700 data files from 24 sources across 6 diverse domains; includes dirty, multi-file data typical of real-world scenarios
Comprehensive evaluation design with three modes (end-to-end, design, implementation) providing nuanced view of system capabilities; demonstrates design reasoning is easier than implementation
Thorough empirical evaluation across 8 systems (6 LLMs + 2 proprietary services) with clear per-domain analysis identifying domain-specific challenges (e.g., astronomy data preparation)
Well-executed benchmark validation: tasks verified through reference implementations and independent reconstruction by annotators to catch ambiguities
Clear presentation with effective use of examples (Figure 1) and structured tables showing breakdown of capabilities and failure modes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DS-GURU baseline applies standard techniques (chain-of-thought, error loops, data sampling) without new methodological contributions; primarily benchmarking paper rather than methodological advance

Relatively small benchmark size (104 tasks) with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs; high potential variance in per-domain results (e.g., Archaeology/Astronomy: 12 tasks each)
LLM-based pipeline evaluation (Section 3.2) lacks validation; using LLMs to judge code correctness is subjective and inter-rater reliability with humans is not reported
Mixed evaluation metrics (Table 3) make cross-task aggregation problematic: different answer types use incomparable schemes (binary vs F1 vs error-based), limiting interpretation of overall scores
Data contamination risk inadequately addressed: wildfire tasks score 3-4x higher even in naive setting (suggesting training data inclusion); OpenAI Deep Research footnote admits web scraping

Limited actionable insights: paper shows systems perform poorly (best 22.08%) but provides little guidance on specific bottlenecks or how to improve systems; unclear if difficulty is inherent or requires better architecture

Shallow failure analysis: no systematic categorization of failure modes, no ablation studies on factors driving difficulty (file count vs. data complexity vs. domain knowledge), limited investigation of why wildfire tasks are much easier

Baseline system quality: DS-GURU is simple; self-correcting variant provides limited benefit over zero-shot (per Section 5.3), suggesting baseline may not be well-tuned compared to recent sophisticated agents
Incomplete presentation: abstract contains placeholder text ('XX real-world systems'), some tables have unclear cells, runtime/compute requirements minimally specified
Generalization limitations: all domains Western-centric (US/European), no multi-modal tasks, unclear applicability beyond these 6 specific domains; future work relegated to discussion
Task difficulty classification uses simple heuristics (file count, subtask count) rather than empirical validation that these correlate with actual system performance difficulty
Reproducibility concerns: API rate limits, cost considerations, and exact code/data release timeline/terms not specified; cannot fully assess reproducibility from submission

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing genuine gap in end-to-end data science evaluation; prior work focuses on isolated components while this captures realistic, multi-step pipelines with heterogeneous, unclean data
Rigorous curation process grounded in published research: 4-step validation with cross-contributor verification, semi-automated key functionality extraction, and diverse domains (1700 files, 1.7GB)

Comprehensive multi-level evaluation framework (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, sub-task implementation) enables fine-grained failure analysis; multiple input modes (Full, Oracle, Trimmed) systematically isolate bottlenecks

Thorough experimental evaluation across 8 LLMs and 4 systems with ablation studies and data leakage investigation; clear actionable insights (agentic > structured; data-dependent reasoning > retrieval as bottleneck)

Diverse capability profiles across LLMs (GPT-o3 strong at planning/weak at implementation vs DeepSeek-R1 opposite) provide evidence that single-agent approaches are fundamentally limited for this task
High transparency and reproducibility: detailed prompts, curation methodology, promised public artifacts, honest reporting of low absolute performance, and clear acknowledgment of limitations
Practical insights on system architecture (agentic retrieval with iterative refinement achieves 50% vs 22% for structured approach) have immediate relevance for practitioners
weaknesses: Modest benchmark scale (104 tasks, ~17 per domain) is small by modern standards (DS-1000 has 1000+); limits statistical power for domain-specific conclusions and may not be sufficient to drive long-term research progress

Critical evaluation methodology concerns: (1) LLM-as-a-judge for pipeline design coverage lacks validation; (2) key functionalities semi-automatically extracted then manually 'polished' without inter-annotator agreement metrics; (3) six different answer type scoring metrics complicate cross-task aggregation

Unfair experimental comparisons: closed-source systems (OpenAI DR, Gemini) enabled with web search while open-source systems offline; confounds system capabilities; Trimmed mode with ≤10 files artificially constrains retrieval-heavy approaches; no error bars despite stochastic LLM sampling

Shallow failure analysis: only 2 detailed case studies of 104 tasks; 'failure to ask for clarification' (24-43%) identified but not explored; no systematic categorization of failure modes; limited guidance on how to translate findings into research directions

Data leakage study limited to 2 domains with inconsistent patterns (Obscured > Full on DS-Guru legal suggests confounds); only 20% obscured; approach (synthetic replacement) may not capture memorization of task structure; doesn't test generalization to novel domains

Incomplete baseline and ablation analysis: no human performance baseline; no comparison to traditional approaches (manual pandas, rule-based retrieval); limited hyperparameter exploration (few-shot correction yields only 1.28% improvement); cost analysis incomplete (smolagents 6.10 min/task vs 0.76 overlooked in discussion)
Limited scope: English-only, tabular/semi-structured data only, Western-centric domains; no multilingual or multimodal evaluation despite acknowledging these gaps

Diminished technical novelty: DS-Guru combines standard techniques (OPS, chain-of-thought, few-shot) without significant innovation; reference system intentionally minimal but limits insights into better approaches; most results show vanilla configurations

strengths: Addresses a genuine benchmarking gap by focusing on end-to-end data science pipelines rather than isolated tasks, which is well-motivated and practically relevant
Rigorous and transparent benchmark curation process with 4-step validation including cross-contributor verification and manual quality control
Comprehensive three-tiered evaluation framework (end-to-end automation, pipeline design, sub-task implementation) provides nuanced assessment
Extensive empirical evaluation with multiple systems, configurations, and ablation studies demonstrates significant effort
Real-world grounding through tasks derived from published studies and complete, publicly accessible datasets
Full reproducibility artifacts including code, data, evaluation scripts, and detailed appendices
Careful attention to data leakage through obscured inputs (20% of tasks with synthetic replacements)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty; core contribution is data curation rather than new evaluation approaches or frameworks

Significant evaluation methodology concerns: (1) LLM-as-a-judge for pipeline design coverage lacks validation or inter-annotator agreement; (2) Oracle mode provides only weak evidence about retrieval importance (9-10% improvement unexplored)

Unfair system comparisons due to confounded variables: OpenAI DR and Gemini have internet access while others don't; systems differ in retrieval mechanism, input constraints, and control flow simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate causality

Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or power analysis across reported percentages; high variance in results (1.73%-50.73% per domain) without reliability assessment

Insufficient failure analysis: only 2 tasks analyzed in Section 4.2 (not statistically representative); no systematic categorization of failure modes across 104 tasks; claims about 'failure to ask clarification' (24-43%) are anecdotal

Limited scope: 104 tasks across 6 niche scientific domains (archaeology, astronomy, wildfire) with unclear generalization to typical business/industry data science; 9-30 tasks per domain is modest for domain-specific claims

Weak data leakage analysis: only 20% of tasks tested; huge performance variance (10-70%, Table 7) across obscured tasks unexplained; conclusions about prior knowledge (12-16% variation) are speculative without rigorous investigation
Few-shot with 20 iterations improves only 1.27% over 5 iterations (Table 12), raising questions about whether the framework or LLMs fundamentally limit performance—not investigated

Shallow and predictable insights: identified limitations (retrieval issues, reasoning weaknesses, lack of holistic understanding) are well-known in LLM literature; no constructive solutions or directions proposed
Evaluation metric concerns: Relative Absolute Error unstable near zero; F1 for lists ignores semantic correctness; ParaPluie validation reliability unknown; arbitrary answer type definitions

strengths: Addresses a critical gap in benchmarking end-to-end data science pipelines over realistic, heterogeneous data lakes—a practically important but underexplored capability
Rigorous and transparent curation process with real-world grounding: 4-step validation, cross-contributor verification, and publicly available published datasets ensure quality and reproducibility

Comprehensive multi-level evaluation framework with three complementary settings (end-to-end, pipeline design, sub-task implementation) that provide fine-grained diagnostic insights into system capabilities

Insightful empirical findings with practical implications: agentic control flow provides 2.3× improvement; retrieval is bottleneck but not primary failure mode; data-dependent reasoning is fundamental challenge; different models have complementary strengths
Thorough experimental analysis including ablation studies on retrieval mechanisms, sample sensitivity, data leakage via obscured inputs, and detailed failure case analysis with concrete examples
Strong reproducibility commitment with full artifacts promised, comprehensive appendices with task details, and reference implementation (DS-Guru) for future research
Clear relevance to high-impact sub-area of AI (data science automation) with actionable insights for system design and identified research directions
weaknesses: Limited domain diversity: only 6 STEM/environment-focused domains with no business, social science, or healthcare tasks; English-only limits global applicability; benchmark size is modest (104 tasks, ~17 per domain) with small domains (Biomedical 9, Astronomy 12) reducing statistical reliability

Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-judge for pipeline design is potentially circular and subjective without inter-rater agreement validation; key functionality identification via instruction-tuned GPT-o3 may bias evaluation toward reference implementation patterns; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Inconsistent system comparison conditions: OpenAI DR and Gemini Agentic evaluated manually via web interface with unenforced web search restrictions versus other systems via offline API; file upload constraints (≤10 for closed-source, full for open-source) confound comparisons

Data leakage analysis insufficient: obscuration strategy is limited (structural patterns remain), only 20% of tasks obscured, counter-intuitive results (obscured improving performance) unexplained, 12-16% degradation lacks contextualization

Large gap between reference implementation (22% best) and best system (50%) raises questions about whether structured approach underperformance reflects fundamental limitations or suboptimal implementation; limited exploration of prompting strategies or retrieval mechanisms for DS-Guru

Limited analysis depth: only 2 detailed failure cases examined; 'failure to ask clarification' insight (24-43%) barely discussed; domain-level performance variation lacks explanation; no systematic error categorization; no inter-annotator agreement for sub-task creation

Incomplete cost analysis with runtime cost only fully reported for one configuration; no cost/accuracy tradeoffs or computational sustainability discussion; benchmark saturation risk not addressed as LLM capabilities improve

Generalization and broader impact limitations: unclear how findings extend beyond these 6 domains; limited practical guidance for practitioners; no discussion of implications for data science education or how alternative valid solutions would be evaluated
